content: Chemicals that disrupt hormones may leave a molecular “scar” that could someday help identify people at higher risk of breast cancer, research in human breast tissue models suggests. People are typically exposed to several chemicals at once, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals that can interfere with the body’s hormones. Scientists have increasingly questioned whether these exposures contribute to breast cancer risk. Much of the evidence, however, comes from animal models or laboratory-grown cells that cannot fully reproduce the complexity of human breast tissue. Researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine and Boston University investigated those effects using three-dimensional models of normal human breast tissue called organoids. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , found that three common bisphenols, BPA, BPS, and BPF, produced relatively few changes when tested individually. When combined at very low concentrations comparable to levels detected in human blood and urine, the chemicals disrupted normal development in organoids from most of the tissue donors. The organoids were grown from breast tissue donated by 13 healthy young women. They contain multiple types of breast cells and can reproduce some aspects of human breast tissue development, allowing researchers to examine chemical exposures during that process. “The breast also is unusual in that it undergoes major developmental changes well after birth, including during puberty and pregnancy,” said Charlotte Kuperwasser, the study’s senior author and a professor of developmental, molecular, and chemical biology at Tufts University School of Medicine. “And the concern is that breast tissue cells may be highly sensitive to environmental cues, such as chemical exposure, during critical windows of mammary gland development.” As the organoids developed over about three weeks, the team exposed them to individual chemicals and mixtures. The panel included substances that disrupt hormones, chemicals that affect metabolism, and known or suspected carcinogens. Researchers then analyzed changes in gene activity and DNA modifications. Different chemicals affected development in different ways, with the bisphenol mixture producing the most striking finding. “We intentionally used concentrations of chemicals that were relevant to real-world exposure rather than the very high doses sometimes used in toxicology studies,” said Kuperwasser. “We also tested a mixture of these because people are typically exposed to multiple chemicals at the same time.” To explore how the changes associated with the bisphenol mixture might relate to disease, the team compared them with molecular data from human breast cancers. The exposure-associated pattern was most strongly represented in data from patients with invasive lobular carcinoma, a type of breast cancer that may not produce a detectable lump and can be difficult to detect with a mammogram. That resemblance does not establish that the chemicals cause cancer or explain how the observed changes might contribute to breast disease. The researchers instead describe the work as a new way to investigate how environmental exposures affect normal human tissue before cancer develops. “Historically, we have thought about cancer risk largely in terms of inherited mutations, lifestyle factors, and exposures that directly damage DNA,” said Kuperwasser. “These findings raise another possibility: Environmental exposures may subtly alter how normal tissues develop, leaving behind molecular changes that do not cause cancer by themselves but may make the tissue more permissive to cancer many years later.” Kuperwasser noted that persistent molecular changes could eventually serve as a biological record, like a “scar” of past exposure. If validated in people, such markers could potentially help identify individuals at higher risk of breast cancer and guide earlier or more targeted screening. “If these results are validated by additional studies, they could change how we think about cancer prevention,” said Kuperwasser. Studies involving larger and more diverse groups of donors, along with a broader range of chemicals and mixtures, are needed to determine how widely the findings apply. Researchers also need to establish whether the molecular changes seen in organoids persist in human tissues and whether they are associated with, or contribute to, breast disease later in life. Reference: “Environmental chemical mixtures reprogram mammary epithelial development to epigenetic states associated with breast cancer” by Meadow Parrish, Meloryn Seraj, Helia Nikoueian, Nicole Traugh, Andrew Chen, Piyush B. Gupta, Stefano Monti and Charlotte Kuperwasser, 15 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2613054123 Supported by Find The Cause Breast Cancer Foundation. content: Scientists have uncovered new clues about the evolution of a rare, deadly Brazilian virus that has circulated largely undetected for more than a century. A rare and deadly virus went undetected in Brazil after genetic changes allowed it to escape existing laboratory tests. Scientists investigating two fatal infections have now identified the mutations responsible, developed an improved detection method, and uncovered evidence that the pathogen has circulated in the country for more than a century. The Sabiá virus can cause severe hemorrhagic and neurological illness, yet only four fatal cases have been documented in São Paulo state since 1990. New genomic research, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases , suggests that additional infections may have escaped diagnosis. The investigation focused on two infections identified in 2019 and 2020. Researchers recovered viral genomes that were approximately 89% genetically identical to strains described in 1999. Crucially, some mutations affected the regions recognized by the DNA primers used in diagnostic tests, preventing those tests from detecting the circulating virus. “The reference strain of the Sabiá virus dates back to 1990, from a case in Cotia. The diagnostic method was developed based on that genome. Since more than 30 years have passed, it was very likely that the virus had mutated. We don’t have enough cases to validate this method further, but it can be used for future suspected cases with greater accuracy than the tests used until now,” says Ingra Morales Claro, who conducted the research during her doctoral studies at the University of São Paulo Medical School (FM-USP) with a FAPESP scholarship. She is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Kentucky. “When analyzing the genomes of the new cases, we identified mutations in target regions of the primers that prevented detection by existing diagnostic tests. We modified those regions, and now it’s possible to identify the circulating strains,” Claro explains. The redesigned primers have been sent to the Adolpho Lutz Institute, a major public health laboratory in São Paulo. One case involved a 52-year-old man from Sorocaba who had a history of hiking in forested areas. He sought medical attention on December 30, 2019, and was transferred to the Hospital das Clínicas (Hospital das Clínicas) in São Paulo with suspected yellow fever. Initial tests for yellow fever and Sabiá virus were negative, and he died on January 11, 2020. Researchers eventually detected Sabiá virus in his blood using metagenomic analysis, which searches for genetic material from multiple microorganisms without requiring scientists to identify a particular pathogen in advance. The rapid approach had been developed during Claro’s doctoral research to detect emerging pathogens in clinical samples. The discovery prompted the team to examine blood samples from seven earlier patients with acute hemorrhagic and neurological illness who had tested negative for yellow fever. One sample revealed another Sabiá infection in a 63-year-old rural worker from Assis. He had been admitted to the Hospital das Clínicas on December 10, 2019, and died two days later. Analysis of the newly recovered genomes identified changes in a viral protein involved in binding to human cells. Although these alterations could be relevant to how the virus interacts with its hosts, the study did not establish whether they changed its ability to infect people or cause severe disease. The researchers also reconstructed the virus’s evolutionary history using phylogenetic analysis, which compares genetic differences to estimate relationships between viral lineages. Their findings suggest that Sabiá has been circulating in Brazil for approximately 142 years, rather than representing a recent introduction. “There were likely other cases in the past that went unidentified. It’s important to understand the virus, develop tests, and study the changes occurring in its genome so that we can anticipate future cases, and even outbreaks, of the disease,” warns Ester Sabino, a professor at FM-USP who coordinates the Brazil-UK Joint Center for Arbovirus Discovery, Diagnostics, Genomics, and Epidemiology (CADDE) in Brazil. Scientists have not established which animal species naturally maintains Sabiá virus, although wild rodents are considered possible reservoirs. The known infections occurred in rural settings where people may encounter wildlife, but the precise route of transmission remains uncertain. The investigation was carried out by CADDE researchers affiliated with FM-USP and Imperial College London, with support from FAPESP . The center has also contributed to genomic investigations of SARS-CoV-2, Zika, mpox, and yellow fever. Sabino helped lead Brazil’s first sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 in March 2020 and subsequent sequencing of mpox in 2022. Nuno Faria, who coordinates CADDE’s UK team, has worked on genomic surveillance of Zika, yellow fever, and the SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant. “In this context, metagenomic approaches have proven to be essential tools for detecting rare or unexpected pathogens, especially when targeted diagnostic tests fail. This strategy was fundamental in identifying both fatal cases of Sabiá in humans and in wild animals, and it highlights the essential role of genomic surveillance in detecting public health risks,” says Faria, referring also to the group’s research on yellow fever evolution and transmission in Brazil. Studying Sabiá virus presents unusual laboratory safety challenges. It is considered one of the Brazilian viruses with the greatest risk of transmission through infectious aerosols in laboratory settings. Handling the active virus requires the highest level of biosafety containment, which is not currently available in South America. Brazil plans to address that limitation with Orion, a laboratory being built at the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM) in Campinas. Scheduled to open in 2030, it will be the country’s first facility equipped to store and handle active Sabiá virus. The reference strain is currently held in the United States. Reference: “Genomic characterization of Sabiá virus in Brazil, 2019–2020: Implications for diagnostics, virus evolution, and receptor binding” by Ingra M. Claro, Erika R. Manuli, Camila A. title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
content:
A new personalised cancer vaccine given alongside a widely used immunotherapy drug has cut the risk of patients dying or their skin cancer returning by 42% in a major clinical trial.
The researchers involved say the results could mark a turning point in cancer treatment, bringing personalised medicine a step closer.
The trial also found that the new drug combination reduced the risk of melanoma, a type of skin cancer, spreading by 38% over two years compared to immunotherapy alone.
The drug manufacturers MSD and Moderna say the same approach is already being tested against other tumours, including kidney, bladder and lung cancer.
Independent cancer experts described the results as impressive but said longer-term studies were still needed to establish whether the treatment really helps most patients live longer, on average.
The new approach is aimed at cancer patients who have already had their tumour removed through surgery.
In the trial, 1,137 adults were given Keytruda, an established immunotherapy drug which helps the body's immune system find and attack cancer cells.
About two-thirds also received an experimental vaccine with the rest being given a placebo or dummy drug.
The vaccine, called Intismeran, uses the same mRNA technology as some Covid jabs.
It is personalised to each patient, using information from their own tumour to help train their immune system to recognise cancer cells and target them if they return.
Two years after starting the treatment, the patients who received the jab were far less likely to have had melanoma come back or see it spread across the body.
"Personalisation is the next step up and it's really exciting, it's a fabulous technology," says Prof Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist who helped run part of the study with patients at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge.
"The question is how much can we really demonstrate its worth and this trial was the first proof of principle."
Prof Corrie worked with patients enrolled in the trial including 75-year old Tony Chapman, who was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019.
He had the tumour removed from his chest but a lump later appeared under his arm. He was told his cancer had returned and he needed a second operation.
He then volunteered to take part in the study but, like all the other participants, he still doesn't know whether he was given the experimental vaccine or a placebo alongside his immunotherapy treatment.
"This just seemed like a really good example of moving science forward, as well as getting some benefit for yourself, so what's to lose?" Tony said.
Three years on he is now having checks every six months and remains cancer-free.
Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer.
But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial.
ranking_reason: Major scientific and technological breakthrough in cancer treatment.

analysis.reason: Major scientific and technological breakthrough in cancer treatment.

final_quality.reason: Substantive, important development in cancer treatment with potential to improve patient outcomes, providing clear reasons for readers to care.
